source_metadata.title: Artificial Intelligence Can Match Domain Experts in Evidence Extraction and Critical Appraisal of Microbial Oncogenesis Research Publications
source_metadata.extraction_scope: Main text and methodologically relevant supplementary material were inspected. Reference-list pages were treated as provenance infrastructure rather than atom targets.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to benchmark four pre-trained reasoning LLMs against domain experts for structured extraction and critical appraisal of biomedical research papers using HMTV/MMTV-like virus and breast cancer as the validation case.
The authors evaluated whether LLMs could interpret nuanced biomedical language.
The authors evaluated whether LLMs could critically appraise biomedical research.
The authors evaluated whether LLMs could apply microbial oncogenesis causal criteria to expert standards.
The authors evaluated whether LLMs could produce accurate and trustworthy outputs with minimal hallucinations or omissions.

The extraction template comprised six sections: Relevancy, Paper Bibliographic Details, Paper Integrity and Reliability, Summary of Paper Contents, Strength of Evidence, and Microbial Oncogenesis Criteria.
The extraction template included 22 multiple-choice questions, four Likert scales, 10 multi-select questions, and 40 long-answer questions.
All MCQs, all Likert scales, and 14 long-answer questions were mandatory; 26 long-answer and all 10 multi-select questions were conditional.
The benchmark dataset comprised 24 original research papers relevant to HMTV/MMTV-like virus and breast cancer.

population.label: Original research papers in the HMTV/MMTV-like virus-breast cancer benchmark

atoms.canonical_statement: The 24 papers consisted of 20 clearly relevant papers from a prior classification dataset plus four additional papers selected for unique and nuanced study designs.

The HMTV/MMTV-like virus-breast cancer pair was selected because its human carcinogenicity is unconfirmed, its evidence is conflicting, African evidence is limited, and its literature includes both human and animal research.
Seven domain experts spanning oncology, clinical microbiology, pathology, infectious diseases, and virology contributed expert annotations, with three experts assigned to each paper.

Questions requiring extensive domain knowledge were answered by three domain experts per paper, whereas objective, extractive, or statistical appraisal questions were answered by one clinician-scientist trainee with data analytics and biostatistics training.
Experts were aware that the study compared LLM and expert responses but were blinded to LLM outputs during annotation.
The evaluated models were Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5, and GPT-5 Nano.
All four evaluated models had context windows of at least 128K tokens and multimodal vision capability.
Default model parameters were used except that the highest available thinking or reasoning effort was selected.
Initial outputs were generated on 17 November 2025 using gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, gpt-5-2025-08-07, and gpt-5-nano-2025-08-07; subsequent experiments used the same APIs.
Each LLM evaluated each of the 24 papers separately in a single API call that supplied the full paper and the complete extraction template; text outputs were converted to JSON for analysis.
If a model classified a paper as not relevant and therefore stopped, the paper was rerun with the relevance-gating instruction removed so that remaining template answers could be assessed.
MCQ agreement was measured as the mean of binary pairwise response matches within each rater group for each question instance, termed the MCQ match proportion.
Likert agreement was measured using average absolute pairwise rating differences, termed scale distance; distances were inverted when scores were combined across question types.
Multi-select questions were excluded from further LLM assessment because experts showed systematic disagreement and models frequently selected all options or answered in prose.
Quantitative and qualitative long-answer assessment used 75 question instances across eight question items for which three valid expert responses were available.
Long-answer pairwise overlap was scored by a GPT-5 LLM judge on a continuous 0-4 scale, and scores were averaged within each rater group for each question instance.
Long-answer completeness was also scored by comparing each LLM response with a reference answer combining all three expert responses on a discrete 0-4 scale.

Manual long-answer review classified expert-LLM gaps as omissions, hallucinations or distortions, or paper-supported additions, using the original paper to distinguish unsupported from supported additions.

Because data were dependent and non-normal, the analysis primarily reported medians and IQRs, used Friedman tests followed by Bonferroni-corrected two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and calculated standardized effect size r when appropriate.

A cross-classified mixed-effects model tested whether individual LLMs preferentially matched specific experts, with LLM identity, expert identity, their interaction, and question type modeled alongside random effects for question and paper.
All analyses were performed using Python 3.14.

In manual validation of 30 pairwise-overlap judgments, the LLM judge exactly matched the human score in 10 cases; 11 additional scores differed by at most 0.5 points, seven by 1 point, and two by 2 points.

atoms.canonical_statement: Expert long-answer responses generally captured similar key points but often emphasized complementary methodological nuances, with methodology-focused questions showing the lowest pairwise overlap.
Inter-LLM long-answer pairwise overlap was significantly greater than inter-expert and expert-LLM overlap, with all pairwise tests p<0.0001 and standardized effect sizes r>0.75.

atoms.canonical_statement: The hallucinations/distortions found in Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-5 Nano occurred exclusively in methodology-focused long-answer questions and represented domain-specific misinterpretations rather than typical fabrications.

GPT-5 Nano produced four unique hallucinations/distortions across seven flagged instances, including errors involving PCR terminology, a 2x2 table, metastatic status, and controls, with some errors affecting evidence-strength appraisal.
Gemini 2.5 Pro classified all 24 benchmark papers as Relevant.
GPT-5 Nano classified 13 of 24 benchmark papers (54.17%) as Somewhat Relevant, the strictest relevance threshold among the models.

LLM relevancy explanations consistently captured the major expert-identified points, with only minor omissions; GPT-5 Nano often downgraded papers lacking temporality or direct causal proof to Somewhat Relevant.
In full-text contradiction detection, Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-5 each identified a human-identified contradiction in only one of 13 contradiction-containing instances.

atoms.canonical_statement: Isolation of contradiction-containing sections substantially improved contradiction detection, which the authors interpreted as evidence that full-text failures were likely related to context limitations rather than inability.
All models rated paper reliability similarly to experts; GPT-5 Nano tended to rate reliability somewhat lower than experts, while Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash were closest to expert reliability scores.

GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash each identified one of four human-identified errors in statistical analysis or result presentation, while the models also identified additional errors missed by the human evaluator.
Across strength-of-evidence ratings, all models had median scale distances of 1 or less from experts; the overall Friedman test was Fr=13.42 with p=0.0197.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that pre-trained reasoning LLMs, particularly GPT-5 and GPT-5 Nano, were indistinguishable from experts across the structured biomedical evidence extraction and appraisal tasks studied.
The authors concluded that reasoning LLMs can support automated evidence synthesis, particularly evidence extraction and integrative summarization of individual biomedical research papers.
The authors identified methodological critique, scoring biases, and full-text contradiction identification as areas requiring further system refinement.

Based on difficulties experienced by both experts and LLMs, the authors recommended replacing multi-select items with binary yes/no statements plus justification fields in future extraction templates.
The evaluation was restricted to a single microbe-cancer pair, limiting confidence that performance generalizes across other evidence profiles or biomedical domains.
The benchmark included only 24 papers, which the authors described as a small sample despite the high number of question-level evaluations.
All seven experts were recruited from a single academic institution, and only three experts evaluated each paper.
Use of a highly structured extraction template may have improved LLM performance and therefore may limit generalizability to less structured prompting or other domains.
Frequent model updates and future deprecation can change or remove the exact model versions evaluated, limiting temporal reproducibility and applicability to newer model families.
Full-text contradiction detection remained weak, while performance improved markedly when relevant sections were isolated; the authors attributed this to context-window or context-rot limitations.

Methodology-focused appraisal questions were a persistent vulnerability: models often omitted sample-size considerations, study-country context, potential errors, or missing information, and smaller models sometimes misinterpreted technical methods.
The study could not directly compare LLM hallucination/error rates with human expert error rates.

The Results and Discussion sections report inconsistent Wilcoxon/effect-size statistics for the aggregate Gemini 2.5 Pro comparison (Results: W=17.0, p=0.0004, r=0.78; Discussion: W=22.0, p<0.0001, r=0.75).
Supplementary Table S1 contains an internal arithmetic inconsistency: the model-row counts imply 14 scores higher than the human judge, whereas the Overall row reports 18.

The study was funded through the South African Medical Research Council Clinician Researcher Development Programme with National Department of Health funding, with additional support from Wits Health Consortium and IDORI; IDORI supported article processing charges.
The authors declared no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
The human-validated test dataset was reported as available in the supplementary material.

extraction_limitations: Atoms preserve the preprint's reported model names, metrics, and statistical claims as published; no external verification was performed.

The paper contains an internal discrepancy in the aggregate Gemini 2.5 Pro Wilcoxon/effect-size statistics between Results and Discussion; both source statements are preserved as separate atoms and flagged.
Supplementary Table S1 has an arithmetic inconsistency in its Overall higher-than-human count; a calculated-from-reported-data limitation atom flags this without altering the source values.
Figure distributions were not reverse-engineered into unreported exact percentages; only values explicitly stated in text, captions, or tables were atomized.
Reference-list entries were not atomized because they are citations to other primary works rather than findings generated by this study.
